summary.text: A histogram is a visual representation of the distribution of quantitative data.
To make one, divide the range of values into consecutive intervals called bins, then count how many values fall into each bin.
A histogram differs from a bar chart: each histogram bin covers a range of values, while each bar in a bar chart stands for a separate category.

facts.label: Bins
facts.value: Adjacent, non-overlapping intervals, typically of equal size

facts.label: Name coined
facts.value: Karl Pearson introduced the term in 1892 lectures

facts.label: Total area
facts.value: Normalized to 1 when used for probability density

facts.label: Bin widths
facts.value: Worth trying several to learn more about the data

items.prompt: You have 200 measured heights and want a histogram. What is the first step?

options.label: Divide the range of heights into intervals
Plot each person as a separate bar
Find the single most common height

items.explain: The first step is to bin the range of values into intervals, then count how many values fall into each.

items.prompt: A chart shows one bar per store so you can compare three different stores. Which chart is it?
items.explain: In a bar chart each bar is a different category, so categories can be compared; a histogram's bins are ranges of values.

items.prompt: Why is it a good idea to plot data with several different bin widths?

options.label: Wider bins are always more correct
To make the total area larger
To avoid counting any value twice
To learn more about the data

items.explain: Plotting with several bin widths shows more about the data than a single choice.

items.prompt: A histogram of exam scores shows two clearly separate peaks. Which word describes that pattern?
items.explain: Words describing histogram patterns include unimodal, bimodal and multimodal; two peaks is bimodal.

items.prompt: Who introduced the word histogram in lectures in 1892?
items.explain: Karl Pearson introduced the term in lectures delivered in 1892 at University College London.

items.prompt: A friend draws bins so one value would be counted in two bins at once. Why is that unusual?

options.label: Bins are usually non-overlapping, so a value falls in one
Bins must always be unequal in size when drawn
Bins are meant to leave gaps between the bars
Each value should be counted twice for safety

items.explain: Bins are usually specified as consecutive, non-overlapping intervals.
